stem: A 72-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer's disease (MMSE 16) on donepezil 10mg for 18 months has become increasingly agitated and aggressive at night. He has no psychotic features. Non-pharmacological strategies (checking for pain, reducing noise at night, low lighting, familiar routine) have been tried without success. He is at risk of being placed in residential care. His wife is exhausted. ECG shows QTc 445ms. He has mild hypertension (controlled on amlodipine). Which is the MOST appropriate pharmacological management?
options: Increase donepezil to 15mg daily — higher dose may improve BPSD
Start risperidone 0.25mg nocte for up to 12 weeks — after discussing increased stroke risk
Start lorazepam 0.5mg nocte PRN for sleep
distractors_rationale: Donepezil is already at maximum licensed dose (10mg). Increasing it would not improve BPSD and would increase cholinergic side effects (nausea, diarrhoea, bradycardia).

CORRECT. For SEVERE BPSD (agitation/aggression) where non-pharmacological measures have failed, NICE NG97 recommends: RISPERIDONE 0.25-0.5mg daily (max 1mg) for up to 12 WEEKS. Key steps: (1) Discuss CVA risk (≈3×) and mortality (≈1.5×) with the wife and DOCUMENT. (2) Start at 0.25mg nocte (can help with sleep). (3) Review at 4 weeks — if no benefit, discontinue. (4) Monitor: EPS, sedation, QTc, metabolic. (5) Attempt to withdraw after 12 weeks. Risk factors for CVA on risperidone: pre-existing CVD (this patient has hypertension), diabetes, age >80. Citalopram and trazodone are options for mild-moderate agitation but risperidone has the strongest evidence for SEVERE aggression/agitation. The 2017 NICE review and multiple RCTs (De Deyn et al., 1999; Katz et al., 1999) support risperidone.

Lorazepam is NOT recommended for BPSD (NICE NG97). Benzodiazepines cause: daytime sedation, paradoxical disinhibition (worse agitation), tolerance, dependence, falls (especially in elderly on antihypertensives). Avoid.

Citalopram has SOME evidence for agitation in dementia (CitAD trial, 2014 — showed benefit for agitation but not for psychosis) but is NOT first-line for SEVERE aggression with risk of residential placement. It also carries QTc prolongation risk >20mg. Risperidone has the strongest evidence base for acute severe agitation/aggression in dementia.

Trazodone (sedating antidepressant) has some evidence for sleep and agitation in dementia but is not first-line for severe aggression. Low-dose (25-50mg nocte) is a reasonable alternative if risperidone is not tolerated or contraindicated. However, risperidone is the most evidence-based option.
teaching_point: BPSD management — NICE NG97 summary: (1) ASSESS: check for pain, infection, constipation, hunger, thirst, sensory, over/understimulation, fear, boredom, medication side effects. (2) NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL FIRST: personalised activities, music therapy, sensory stimulation (aromatherapy, massage), environmental modifications, carer training (de-escalation, communication). (3) PHARMACOLOGICAL — ONLY if severe and non-pharm failed: Risperidone 0.25-1mg (max 12 weeks). Discuss CVA risk (≈3×) and mortality (≈1.5×). Review at 4 weeks. STOP after 12 weeks. (4) Antidepressants: citalopram (10-20mg) for agitation WITHOUT psychosis (off-label); trazodone (25-100mg) for sleep/agitation. (5) AVOID: benzodiazepines (except emergencies), valproate (no evidence), polypharmacy. (6) The DEPENDENT factors (family carer): support the carer, offer training, allow respite. The 'MEDICAL CAUSES': DELIRIUM is a common cause of acute worsening in dementia — always check for infection, electrolyte, acute illness.
source: NICE NG97: Dementia; Ballard C et al. (2009) Antipsychotics in dementia; BNF

stem:
Theme: Offence-Specific Knowledge in Forensic Psychiatry

For each type of crime, select the MOST LIKELY PSYCHIATRIC ASSOCIATION:

A. Antisocial personality disorder + alcohol misuse
B. Schizophrenia (paranoid) with persecutory delusions
C. Stalking — erotomania (de Clérambault's syndrome)
D. Pathological gambling
E. Munchausen syndrome by proxy (factitious disorder imposed on another)
F. Malingering
G. Morbid jealousy (Othello syndrome)
H. Diminished responsibility (depression)
I. Delirium tremens
J. Alcohol hallucinosis
K. Pyromania
L. Kleptomania
options: A 45-year-old woman with history of multiple hospital presentations of her child with fabricated symptoms (apnoea, seizures, fever) despite extensive negative investigations. No personal gain is identified.
A 35-year-old man is convinced his wife is having an affair despite no evidence. He checks her phone, follows her, and has threatened to kill her. One evening he attacks her with a knife.

A 28-year-old woman develops the fixed belief that a television presenter is in love with her. She has sent hundreds of letters, travelled to his home, and waited outside his house. She has no other psychotic symptoms.

A 55-year-old man with a history of three DTs-related admissions and multiple detoxifications is charged with assault after striking a stranger who he believed was trying to kill him during an episode of delirium tremens.
distractors_rationale: MUNCHAUSEN SYNDROME BY PROXY (E) — now called FACTITIOUS DISORDER IMPOSED ON ANOTHER (FDIA) in DSM-5-TR. The parent (usually mother) fabricates or induces illness in a child, for the purpose of GAINING ATTENTION AS A CAREGIVER (the 'sick role by proxy'). There is NO EXTERNAL INCENTIVE (unlike malingering). The motive is to fulfil the parent's own emotional needs through the sick role. RED FLAGS: (1) History of multiple, unexplained or bizarre symptoms; (2) Symptoms only happen in the mother's presence; (3) Mother is overly attentive, refuses to leave the child, and appears knowledgeable about medical terminology; (4) The child has had multiple investigations and procedures; (5) Mother has a history of FDIA or somatization herself. RISK: the child can suffer serious harm and may be killed. MANAGEMENT: safeguarding referral, child protection, MDT assessment, limit-setting, psychological therapy for the mother. LEGAL: the mother can be charged with assault/causing harm.

MORBID JEALOUSY — OTHELLO SYNDROME (G). A delusional belief that a partner is unfaithful, WITHOUT sufficient evidence. It can occur in: psychotic disorders (schizophrenia, delusional disorder — 'delusional jealousy'), dementia, substance misuse (alcohol, cocaine — 'when drunk, he accuses her of affairs'), organic conditions (Parkinson's, TBI). It carries a HIGH RISK OF VIOLENCE towards the partner (the attack reflects the high risk). The person may try to: (1) Check phone/clothes; (2) Follow the partner; (3) Confront the alleged lover; (4) Attack the partner (the attack in the scenario). Management: (1) Treat the underlying disorder (antipsychotic if psychotic; consider alcohol/cessation); (2) Risk assessment (HCR-20); (3) Safety planning for the partner. Othello syndrome complicates about 5% of psychotic disorders. The person may also harm the partner's children or family members.

EROTOMANIA (DE CLÉRAMBAULT'S SYNDROME) (C). The delusional belief that a person (usually of higher social status) is IN LOVE with the individual. The person may believe the object of delusion is sending secret messages (through TV, gestures). They may write letters, make phone calls, approach the person, or stalk them. Associated with: delusional disorder (erotomanic type), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder (manic). De Clérambault's syndrome: the prototypical erotomania. Stalking: RATIONALE — if the belief is delusional (erotomania), the person may need treatment with antipsychotics. If it is obsessional (not delusional), treatment may include SSRIs and CBT.

DELIRIUM TREMENS (I) — but this is a medical condition, not a psychiatric diagnosis per se. DTs (alcohol withdrawal delirium) can lead to VIOLENCE driven by: (1) Frightening visual hallucinations (insects, animals); (2) Paranoia (believing others are trying to harm him); (3) CONFUSION. The person is suffering from a MEDICAL EMERGENCY (DTs mortality ~5%). In LEGAL TERMS: (1) This could be a defence of NON-INSANE AUTOMATISM (if the act was involuntary due to an acute confusional state) OR (2) The M'Naghten Rules may apply if the person was so confused that they did not know the nature and quality of their act. However, voluntary alcohol intoxication does NOT provide a defence — it is the DELIRIUM (disease of the mind) that may provide a defence.
teaching_point: Forensic psychiatry — HIGH-YIELD syndromes: (1) OTHELLO SYNDROME (morbid jealousy): delusion of infidelity, high violence risk towards partner. (2) DE CLÉRAMBAULT'S (erotomania): delusion that someone is in love with you. (3) MUNCHAUSEN BY PROXY (FDIA): fabricating illness in another for attention. (4) MUNCHAUSEN SYNDROME: fabricating illness in oneself. (5) CAPGRAS SYNDROME: belief that a person (usually close) has been replaced by an identical imposter. (6) FREGOLI SYNDROME: belief that different people are the same person in disguise. (7) COTARD'S SYNDROME: nihilistic delusion that the person does not exist or is dead. (8) LYNCANTHROPY: belief that one can transform into an animal. (9) REDUPLICATIVE PARAMNESIA: belief that a place has been duplicated. M'Naghten defence: insanity (defect of reason from disease of the mind — did not know nature/quality or wrongness). Automatism: involuntary act (non-insane = external cause → complete acquittal; insane = internal cause → NGRI).
source: MHA 1983; M'Naghten Rules (1843); DSM-5-TR; Criminal Procedure (Insanity) Act 1964

stem: A 42-year-old man with schizophrenia (well-controlled on clozapine 400mg daily) is brought to the emergency department by police under Section 136 after shouting at strangers in the street. He is known to the mental health team — his clozapine levels have been therapeutic and he has been stable for 18 months. He refuses to stay informally. In the ED, he is alert, oriented, and says he was shouting because a stranger stepped on his foot and he was angry. He says he is not unwell and wants to leave. He is not suicidal or homicidal. The S136 assessment is initiated. The approved mental health professional (AMHP) and the two doctors assess him and find he does NOT meet criteria for detention under the MHA (no current mental disorder requiring detention). What happens NEXT?
options: He can be detained under S136 for up to 24 hours for further observation
He must be RELEASED immediately — the S136 assessment is complete and he does not meet criteria for detention
He should be started on emergency antipsychotic medication
He should be transferred to a psychiatric intensive care unit
The police can detain him for up to 12 hours for 'breach of the peace'
distractors_rationale: The S136 assessment has been completed (AMHP + 2 doctors) and the conclusion is that he does NOT meet criteria for detention. The maximum detention period is for the PURPOSE OF THE ASSESSMENT — once the assessment is complete and the person does not meet criteria, they MUST be RELEASED (MHA 1983, Code of Practice, Paragraph 16.62).

CORRECT. The legal position is clear: Section 136 authorises detention for the PURPOSE OF ASSESSMENT. Once the assessment has been completed and the person is found NOT to have a mental disorder warranting detention, the legal authority ENDS. The person MUST be discharged immediately. The mental health team cannot detain someone simply for observation if they do not meet MHA criteria. If the person is willing to stay informally, they can. If not, they must be released. The police cannot detain him under S136 for a longer period. In this case, the person's behaviour (shouting) was explained by a PROPORTIONATE RESPONSE to a physical event (being stepped on), not by mental disorder. His schizophrenia is well-controlled. The MHA is not a 'preventative' detention power — it requires a current mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention. NMS (No Mental Disorder) — the person must be discharged.
There is no indication for emergency medication — he is not acutely unwell and the behaviour was explained.
PICU would only be appropriate if he was compulsorily detained, which he is not.
Section 136 is the emergency application — once it is exhausted, breach of the peace cannot be used to circumvent MHA protections.
teaching_point: Section 136 — the process: (1) REMOVAL: police remove a person from a public place to a place of safety (preferably hospital, not police station). Duration: up to 24 hours (extendable by 12 hours if assessment cannot be completed). (2) ASSESSMENT: by TWO doctors (one S12 approved) and an AMHP. (3) OUTCOMES: (a) Application for detention (S2 or S3) — if criteria met; (b) RELEASE — if no mental disorder requiring detention, OR person agrees to stay informally; (c) Referral to community services — if ongoing care needs but not detention. (4) CHILDREN: must not be taken to a police station (Policing and Crime Act 2017). (5) AFTER RELEASE: the person should be offered information about their rights, a written care plan, and signposting to appropriate services (GP, CMHT, crisis service). The MHA Code of Practice (2015) is clear: the purpose of S136 is to enable a MENTAL HEALTH ASSESSMENT — not for 'observation' or 'preventative' purposes. Once the assessment concludes the person does not need detention, they MUST be released.
source: MHA 1983; MHA Code of Practice (2015); Policing and Crime Act 2017

stem: A 22-year-old woman with a history of cannabis use presents with a 6-week history of paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations (voices commenting). She has no previous psychiatric history, no mood symptoms, and no substance use in the past 4 weeks. Urine drug screen is negative. She is started on aripiprazole 10mg daily. After 4 weeks, her PANSS positive score has reduced by only 10%, and she continues to experience significant persecutory beliefs. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Increase aripiprazole to 15mg and continue for another 4 weeks
Switch to olanzapine 10mg daily immediately because aripiprazole is clearly ineffective
Diagnose treatment-resistant schizophrenia and start clozapine
Add cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp) and continue aripiprazole — 4 weeks may not be enough for full response
distractors_rationale: CORRECT. According to NICE CG178, the response to an antipsychotic should be assessed after 4-6 WEEKS at an ADEQUATE THERAPEUTIC DOSE. Aripiprazole 10mg is within the therapeutic range but the MAXIMUM LICENSED DOSE is 30mg. The patient has had ONLY a PARTIAL RESPONSE (10% PANSS reduction). The correct management at 4 weeks with partial response is: (1) INCREASE THE DOSE (if tolerated) and continue for ANOTHER 4-6 weeks to allow FULL response; (2) Assess adherence (check levels if possible); (3) Add psychological therapy (CBTp). Treatment resistance is defined as FAILURE OF TWO ADEQUATE TRIALS of different antipsychotics at adequate doses for ≥6 weeks. This patient has had ONLY ONE TRIAL and for only 4 weeks — clozapine would be premature.
Switching at 4 weeks is PREMATURE. Aripiprazole needs to be optimised (dose increased) and given a full 6-8 week trial.
Treatment resistance requires TWO failed antipsychotic trials of adequate dose and duration (≥6 weeks). This patient has had ONE TRIAL for 4 WEEKS — too early for clozapine.
CBTp should be offered alongside medication but should not replace optimising the dose.
Lithium augmentation for schizophrenia is an option for clozapine-resistant or clozapine-augmented treatment, not for a first trial with only 4 weeks of treatment.
teaching_point: Antipsychotic response assessment: (1) FULL RESPONSE: >20% reduction in PANSS/BPRS + CGI improvement, 4-6 weeks at adequate dose. (2) PARTIAL RESPONSE (10-20%): increase dose (if tolerated) and continue for 4-6 more weeks + add CBTp. (3) NO RESPONSE (<10%): switch to a DIFFERENT class antipsychotic. (4) SECOND FAILURE: consider treatment resistance → clozapine. (5) DEFINITION OF TREATMENT RESISTANCE: NICE CG178 — 'little or no improvement despite adequate trials (≥6 weeks at therapeutic dose) of at least two different antipsychotics.' The Kane criteria (1988): (1) No period of good functioning in the past 5 years; (2) Failure of 3 antipsychotics from ≥2 chemical classes at doses equivalent to ≥1000mg chlorpromazine for 6 weeks; (3) Moderate-severe psychopathology. Aripiprazole therapeutic dose: 10-30mg daily. Time to full response: 6-8 weeks (some studies suggest up to 12 weeks for negative symptoms). The principle: 'Start low, go slow, but get to a THERAPEUTIC DOSE.'
source: NICE CG178: Psychosis and schizophrenia; Kane J et al. (1988) Clozapine for TRS; Maudsley PG
